introduction:
\hypersetup{pageanchor=true}
\pagenumbering{roman}
\section*{About this handbook}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{About this handbook}

This handbook connects recursive programs, state graphs, and dynamic programming
tables through small, fully specified examples. It assumes familiarity with Python,
recursion, and basic graph algorithms. Brief captions identify the dependencies,
evaluation order, and choices visible in each snapshot.

Fibonacci introduces repeated subproblems; knapsack and edit distance compare
alternatives; matrix-chain multiplication combines two required subproblems per
choice. Water jugs and Hanoi expose cycles and shortest-path structure. Two Sets II
closes with three recursive coordinate systems for the same counting problem.

\vspace{3mm}
\section*{How to read the diagrams}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Calls and states.} Repeated arguments give separate occurrences
        in a call tree and a single vertex in a merged state graph.
  \item \textbf{Forward arrows are calls or dependencies.} Faint or dotted edges
        are pending or contextual; stronger edges are currently active.
  \item \textbf{Return labels complete an expression.} A placeholder such as
        \emph{value + ??} becomes \emph{value + returned value} when its child finishes.
  \item \textbf{Emphasis follows the chapter legend.} Gold usually marks an
        optimal choice; in Fibonacci it marks a memoization frontier, and in
        Two Sets II it marks a comparison history.
  \item \textbf{Black partition nodes join required calls.} In matrix-chain
        multiplication they show that one split needs both interval subproblems.
  \item \textbf{Table order follows dependencies.} Blank cells await evaluation;
        disabled cells lie outside the recurrence's state space. Some valid
        table cells are absent from the selected recursive trace.
\end{itemize}
\vspace{3mm}
\noindent\textbf{Acyclic versus cyclic dependencies.}
Memoization reuses a completed value; a visited mark only rejects a cycle on the
current path. In the jug and Hanoi graphs, distance-to-target labels describe
unrestricted shortest paths. A recursive call under an existing visited set may
have fewer admissible continuations.
\clearpage

chapters.title: Fibonacci
chapters.subtitle: The smallest recurrence that reveals repeated work
chapters.summary: Both recursive calls are required. Merging repeated arguments produces a dependency DAG; evaluating it in order produces the DP array.

blocks.title: Problem overview and examples
blocks.body: {\sffamily\fontsize{8.0}{9.2}\selectfont \textbf{Problem.} Compute the $n$th Fibonacci number, with $F(0)=0$, $F(1)=1$, and $F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2)$ for $n\ge2$.\par\vspace{2mm}\textbf{Example 1 (used below).} Input: $n=6$. Output: $8$.\par\vspace{1mm}\textbf{Example 2.} Input: $n=7$. Output: $13$.\par\vspace{2mm}The same recurrence is evaluated as a call tree, a memoized DAG, and a DP array.\par}

blocks.title: Block 01 -- recursive code
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{7.1}{7.9}\selectfont The state is one integer n. Each non-base call must evaluate both recursive values.\par\vspace{1mm}}{\ttfamily\fontsize{6.8}{7.6}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ fib(n):}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ case\ 1.}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{if\ n\ ==\ 0:}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{return\ 0}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ case\ 2.}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{if\ n\ ==\ 1:}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{return\ 1}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{\#\ Recursive\ choices.}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{val1\ =\ fib(n\ -\ 1)}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{val2\ =\ fib(n\ -\ 2)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{return\ val1\ +\ val2}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(fib(6))\ \ \#\ 8}\par
}
blocks.footer: Both child values are required; this recurrence adds results rather than choosing between them.

blocks.title: Block 02 -- call fib(6)
Block 03 -- reach the first completed subproblem
Block 04 -- return fib(4)
Block 05 -- finish fib(5)

Block 07 -- complete naive fib(6)

blocks.title: Memo Block 01 -- top-down memoized code
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{7.1}{7.9}\selectfont memo[n] stores a completed state. A repeated call returns without rebuilding its subtree.\par\vspace{1mm}}{\ttfamily\fontsize{6.2}{7.0}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{N\ =\ 6}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{memo\ =\ [None]\ *\ (N\ +\ 1)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ fib(n):}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ case\ 1.}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{if\ n\ ==\ 0:}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{memo[0]\ =\ 0}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{return\ 0}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ case\ 2.}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{if\ n\ ==\ 1:}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{memo[1]\ =\ 1}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{return\ 1}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{\#\ Reuse\ a\ completed\ subproblem.}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{if\ memo[n]\ is\ not\ None:}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{return\ memo[n]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{val1\ =\ fib(n\ -\ 1)}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{val2\ =\ fib(n\ -\ 2)}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{memo[n]\ =\ val1\ +\ val2}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{return\ memo[n]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(fib(N))\ \ \#\ 8}\par
}
blocks.footer: Each distinct non-base state is expanded once: $O(N)$ time and $O(N)$ cache space.

blocks.title: Bottom-up Block 01 -- array code
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{7.1}{7.9}\selectfont The same recurrence is evaluated in dependency order, beginning with both base cells.\par\vspace{1mm}}{\ttfamily\fontsize{6.5}{7.2}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{N\ =\ 6}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{dp\ =\ [0]\ *\ (N\ +\ 1)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ cases.}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{dp[0]\ =\ 0}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{dp[1]\ =\ 1}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ Fill\ the\ array\ from\ left\ to\ right.}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{for\ n\ in\ range(2,\ N\ +\ 1):}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{val1\ =\ dp[n\ -\ 1]}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{val2\ =\ dp[n\ -\ 2]}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{dp[n]\ =\ val1\ +\ val2}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(dp[N])\ \ \#\ 8}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ Space\ note:\ only\ dp[n-1]\ and\ dp[n-2]\ are\ needed.}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ The\ two-variable\ version\ is\ not\ shown\ here.}\par
}

chapters.title: 0/1 Knapsack
chapters.subtitle: Binary choices, invalid states, and a maximizing table
chapters.summary: Each item offers a take-or-skip decision. The DAG merges equal states; the table evaluates the same maximum from right to left.
chapters.goal: Maximize total value without exceeding capacity.
chapters.base: At the end of the item list, return $0$ for feasible capacity and $-\infty$ otherwise.
chapters.legend: dotted = pending; blue = active call; green = returned node; orange = return edge; purple = cache hit; gold = chosen max edge

blocks.title: Problem overview and examples
blocks.body: {\sffamily\fontsize{6.2}{7.0}\selectfont \textbf{Problem.} Choose a subset of items, using each item at most once, to maximize total value without exceeding the capacity.\par\vspace{.7mm}\textbf{Example 1 (used below).} Weights $[0.1,0.1,0.2]$, values $[3,4,6]$, capacity $0.2$ $\rightarrow$ output $7$ by taking the first two items.\par\vspace{.5mm}\textbf{Example 2.} Weights $[0.2,0.3]$, values $[4,5]$, capacity $0.3$ $\rightarrow$ output $5$.\par}

blocks.title: Plain recursive code; memoized-DAG view
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{6.5}{7.2}\selectfont Every branch reaches \texttt{item == N}; a negative remaining capacity returns $-\infty$.}\par\vspace{1mm}
{\ttfamily\fontsize{5.8}{6.6}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{WT\ =\ [0.1,\ 0.1,\ 0.2]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{VAL\ =\ [3,\ 4,\ 6]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{N\ =\ len(WT)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{NEG\_INF\ =\ float("-inf")}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ knapsack(item,\ remaining):}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{if\ item\ >=\ N:}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{return\ (0\ if\ remaining\ >=\ 0}\par
\hspace*{7.68em}\mbox{else\ NEG\_INF)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{take\ =\ VAL[item]\ +\ knapsack(}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{item\ +\ 1,}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{round(remaining\ -\ WT[item],\ 1))}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{skip\ =\ 0\ +\ knapsack(}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{item\ +\ 1,\ remaining)}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{return\ max(take,\ skip)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(knapsack(0,\ 0.2))\ \ \#\ 7}\par
}
\vfill{\sffamily\fontsize{6.2}{7.0}\selectfont The code remains plain recursion. The figures merge identical states into a DAG and preview the work that memoization would skip.\par}
blocks.footer: Capacities use a $0.1$ grid; rounding preserves this example's states.

blocks.title: Bottom-up code
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{6.4}{7.1}\selectfont All weights are positive, so negative-capacity rows are infeasible. Columns A, AB, ABC denote the next item considered; X marks the terminal column.}\par\vspace{.8mm}
{\ttfamily\fontsize{5.8}{6.6}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{CAPS\ =\ [-0.2,\ -0.1,\ 0.0,\ 0.1,\ 0.2]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{dp\ =\ \{\}}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ Same\ terminal\ rules\ as\ the\ recursion.}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{for\ c\ in\ CAPS:}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{dp[N,\ c]\ =\ 0\ if\ c\ >=\ 0\ else\ NEG\_INF}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{for\ item\ in\ range(N):}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{for\ c\ in\ (-0.2,\ -0.1):}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{dp[item,\ c]\ =\ NEG\_INF}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ Fill\ columns\ right\ to\ left;\ rows\ bottom\ to\ top.}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{for\ item\ in\ range(N\ -\ 1,\ -1,\ -1):}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{for\ c\ in\ (0.0,\ 0.1,\ 0.2):}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{take\_c\ =\ round(c\ -\ WT[item],\ 1)}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{tail\ =\ dp[item\ +\ 1,\ take\_c]}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{take\ =\ (NEG\_INF\ if\ tail\ ==\ NEG\_INF}\par
\hspace*{7.68em}\mbox{else\ VAL[item]\ +\ tail)}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{skip\ =\ dp[item\ +\ 1,\ c]}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{dp[item,\ c]\ =\ max(take,\ skip)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(dp[0,\ 0.2])\ \ \#\ 7}\par
}

chapters.title: Edit Distance
chapters.subtitle: Three-way choices over two string positions
chapters.summary: A suffix pair offers insertion, deletion, or a diagonal match/substitution. The table evaluates all suffix pairs in dependency order.
chapters.goal: Minimize the number of edits that transform one string into the other.
chapters.base: When either suffix is exhausted, return the length of the other suffix.
chapters.legend: dotted = pending; blue = active call; orange = latest return; purple = cache/base; gold = minimum-cost choice

blocks.title: Problem overview and examples
blocks.body: {\sffamily\fontsize{7.5}{8.4}\selectfont \textbf{Problem.} Find the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform one string into another.\par\vspace{1.2mm}\textbf{Example 1 (used below).} Input: \texttt{MOVIE} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{LOVE}. Output: $2$ (substitute M with L, then delete I).\par\vspace{.8mm}\textbf{Example 2.} Input: \texttt{CAT} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{CUT}. Output: $1$.\par}

blocks.title: Plain recursive code; memoized-DAG projection
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{7.2}{8}\selectfont Each interior state evaluates diagonal, delete, and insert. State $(i,j)$ compares the suffixes SOURCE[i:] and TARGET[j:].}\par\vspace{1mm}
{\ttfamily\fontsize{7.0}{7.8}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{SOURCE\ =\ "MOVIE"}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{TARGET\ =\ "LOVE"}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{M,\ N\ =\ len(SOURCE),\ len(TARGET)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ edit\_distance(i,\ j):}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{if\ i\ >=\ M:}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{return\ N\ -\ j}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{if\ j\ >=\ N:}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{return\ M\ -\ i}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{cost\ =\ 0\ if\ SOURCE[i]\ ==\ TARGET[j]\ else\ 1}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{diagonal\ =\ cost\ +\ edit\_distance(i\ +\ 1,\ j\ +\ 1)}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{delete\ =\ 1\ +\ edit\_distance(i\ +\ 1,\ j)}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{insert\ =\ 1\ +\ edit\_distance(i,\ j\ +\ 1)}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{return\ min(diagonal,\ delete,\ insert)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(edit\_distance(0,\ 0))\ \ \#\ 2}\par
}
\vfill{\sffamily\fontsize{6.8}{7.6}\selectfont The naive recursion makes 1,021 calls (2,042 call/return events). The figures merge identical states and show selected milestones.\par}

blocks.title: Bottom-up code
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{7.2}{8}\selectfont The loop order is a topological order of the same state DAG.}\par\vspace{1mm}
{\ttfamily\fontsize{7.0}{7.8}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{SOURCE\ =\ "MOVIE"}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{TARGET\ =\ "LOVE"}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{M,\ N\ =\ len(SOURCE),\ len(TARGET)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{dp\ =\ [[0]\ *\ (N\ +\ 1)\ for\ \_\ in\ range(M\ +\ 1)]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ Separated\ base\ row\ and\ base\ column.}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{for\ j\ in\ range(N,\ -1,\ -1):}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{dp[M][j]\ =\ N\ -\ j}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{for\ i\ in\ range(M,\ -1,\ -1):}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{dp[i][N]\ =\ M\ -\ i}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ Columns\ right\ to\ left;\ cells\ bottom\ to\ top.}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{for\ j\ in\ range(N\ -\ 1,\ -1,\ -1):}\par
\hspace*{1.92em}\mbox{for\ i\ in\ range(M\ -\ 1,\ -1,\ -1):}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{cost\ =\ 0\ if\ SOURCE[i]\ ==\ TARGET[j]\ else\ 1}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{diagonal\ =\ cost\ +\ dp[i\ +\ 1][j\ +\ 1]}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{delete\ =\ 1\ +\ dp[i\ +\ 1][j]}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{insert\ =\ 1\ +\ dp[i][j\ +\ 1]}\par
\hspace*{3.84em}\mbox{dp[i][j]\ =\ min(diagonal,\ delete,\ insert)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(dp[0][0])\ \ \#\ 2}\par
}

chapters.title: Water Jugs: Cyclic State Graphs
chapters.subtitle: When dependencies are no longer a DAG
chapters.summary: Legal moves form a cyclic graph. Path-local cycle rejection makes exhaustive recursion finite; BFS computes shortest distances in linear time in the graph size.
chapters.state: $(a,b)$, the current amounts in the two jugs
chapters.goal: Reach $a+b=\mathit{TARGET}$ in the minimum number of moves.
chapters.base: A target returns $0$; revisiting the current path returns $\infty$.

blocks.title: Problem overview and examples
blocks.body: {\sffamily\fontsize{8.0}{9.1}\selectfont \textbf{Problem.} Two unmarked jugs have fixed capacities. A move may fill a jug, empty a jug, or pour from one jug to the other until the source is empty or the destination is full. Find the minimum number of moves that makes the total water equal the target.\par\vspace{2mm}\textbf{Example 1 (used below).} Capacities $(3,5)$, target total $4$ $\rightarrow$ output $7$.\par\vspace{1mm}\textbf{Example 2.} Capacities $(2,3)$, target total $3$ $\rightarrow$ output $1$ by filling the three-unit jug.\par\vspace{2mm}State $(a,b)$ records the current quantity in each jug. Every legal action costs one move.\par}

blocks.title: Recursive code: explicit cases and path-local cycle rejection
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{7.0}{7.8}\selectfont The goal is the value base case. A repeated state is the cycle base case. All six choices are evaluated independently, and the visited mark is removed before the call returns.}\par\vspace{1.2mm}
{\ttfamily\fontsize{6.10}{6.78}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{from\ math\ import\ inf}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{CAP\_A,\ CAP\_B,\ TARGET\ =\ 3,\ 5,\ 4}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{VISITED\ =\ [[False]\ *\ (CAP\_B\ +\ 1)\ for\ \_\ in\ range(CAP\_A\ +\ 1)]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ moves(a,\ b):}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{pour\_ab\ =\ min(a,\ CAP\_B\ -\ b)}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{pour\_ba\ =\ min(b,\ CAP\_A\ -\ a)}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{return\ (}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{(CAP\_A,\ b),\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ fill\ jug\ A}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{(a,\ CAP\_B),\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ fill\ jug\ B}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{(0,\ b),\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ empty\ jug\ A}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{(a,\ 0),\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ empty\ jug\ B}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{(a\ -\ pour\_ab,\ b\ +\ pour\_ab),\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ pour\ A\ ->\ B}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{(a\ +\ pour\_ba,\ b\ -\ pour\_ba),\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ pour\ B\ ->\ A}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ min\_moves(a,\ b):}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ cases}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{if\ a\ +\ b\ ==\ TARGET:}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{return\ 0}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{if\ VISITED[a][b]:\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ reject\ a\ cyclic\ call}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{return\ inf}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{VISITED[a][b]\ =\ True}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{fill\_a\_state,\ fill\_b\_state,\ empty\_a\_state,\ empty\_b\_state,\ \textbackslash{}}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{a\_to\_b\_state,\ b\_to\_a\_state\ =\ moves(a,\ b)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{def\ call(next\_state):}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{if\ next\_state\ ==\ (a,\ b):\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ reject\ an\ immediate\ no-op}\par
\hspace*{5.40em}\mbox{return\ inf}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{return\ min\_moves(*next\_state)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{\#\ Six\ recursive\ choices,\ kept\ separate\ for\ inspection}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{fill\_a\ =\ call(fill\_a\_state)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ choose:\ fill\ jug\ A}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{fill\_b\ =\ call(fill\_b\_state)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ choose:\ fill\ jug\ B}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{empty\_a\ =\ call(empty\_a\_state)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ choose:\ empty\ jug\ A}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{empty\_b\ =\ call(empty\_b\_state)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ choose:\ empty\ jug\ B}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{a\_to\_b\ =\ call(a\_to\_b\_state)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ choose:\ pour\ A\ ->\ B}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{b\_to\_a\ =\ call(b\_to\_a\_state)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ choose:\ pour\ B\ ->\ A}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{VISITED[a][b]\ =\ False\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ backtrack\ for\ sibling\ choices}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{return\ 1\ +\ min(fill\_a,\ fill\_b,\ empty\_a,}\par
\hspace*{8.55em}\mbox{empty\_b,\ a\_to\_b,\ b\_to\_a)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(min\_moves(0,\ 0))\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ 7}\par
}
\vfill{\sffamily\fontsize{7.0}{7.8}\selectfont Path-local marks permit every simple continuation. They are not memoized values: the admissible continuations depend on the current path.\par}
blocks.footer: At an independent start with an empty VISITED table, the recursion returns the unrestricted shortest distance $r(a,b)$.

blocks.title: Complete state graph: start distances and optimal remaining distances
blocks.footer: The complete graph is cyclic. The gold subgraph is acyclic because every gold edge strictly decreases $r$.

blocks.title: DP code: minimum distance from the empty state
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{6.9}{7.7}\selectfont This is BFS expressed as table relaxation. Each operation remains a separate semantic case, matching the recursion.}\par\vspace{.8mm}
{\ttfamily\fontsize{5.75}{6.43}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{from\ collections\ import\ deque}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{from\ math\ import\ inf}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{CAP\_A,\ CAP\_B,\ TARGET\ =\ 3,\ 5,\ 4}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{dp\ =\ [[inf]\ *\ (CAP\_B\ +\ 1)\ for\ \_\ in\ range(CAP\_A\ +\ 1)]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{dp[0][0]\ =\ 0}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{queue\ =\ deque([(0,\ 0)])}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ relax(a,\ b,\ next\_a,\ next\_b):}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{\#\ Skip\ no-op\ actions\ and\ keep\ only\ strict\ improvements.}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{if\ (next\_a,\ next\_b)\ ==\ (a,\ b):}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{return}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{candidate\ =\ dp[a][b]\ +\ 1}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{if\ candidate\ <\ dp[next\_a][next\_b]:}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{dp[next\_a][next\_b]\ =\ candidate}\par
\hspace*{3.60em}\mbox{queue.append((next\_a,\ next\_b))}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{while\ queue:}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{a,\ b\ =\ queue.popleft()}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{pour\_ab\ =\ min(a,\ CAP\_B\ -\ b)}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{pour\_ba\ =\ min(b,\ CAP\_A\ -\ a)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{\#\ The\ same\ six\ semantic\ cases\ as\ in\ the\ recursion}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{relax(a,\ b,\ CAP\_A,\ b)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ fill\ jug\ A}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{relax(a,\ b,\ a,\ CAP\_B)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ fill\ jug\ B}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{relax(a,\ b,\ 0,\ b)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ empty\ jug\ A}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{relax(a,\ b,\ a,\ 0)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ empty\ jug\ B}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{relax(a,\ b,\ a\ -\ pour\_ab,\ b\ +\ pour\_ab)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ pour\ A\ ->\ B}\par
\hspace*{1.80em}\mbox{relax(a,\ b,\ a\ +\ pour\_ba,\ b\ -\ pour\_ba)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ pour\ B\ ->\ A}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{answer\ =\ min(dp[a][b]}\par
\hspace*{5.85em}\mbox{for\ a\ in\ range(CAP\_A\ +\ 1)}\par
\hspace*{5.85em}\mbox{for\ b\ in\ range(CAP\_B\ +\ 1)}\par
\hspace*{5.85em}\mbox{if\ a\ +\ b\ ==\ TARGET)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(answer)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ 7}\par
}
blocks.footer: Unit-cost BFS takes $O(V+E)$ time and $O(V)$ space. Here $V=24$ and $E=106$ distinct transitions.

blocks.title: Final distance table with a visible three-state cycle
blocks.footer: Red cycle: $(0,0)\to(3,0)\to(0,3)\to(0,0)$. Edge annotations report destination distances $d'$; relaxation compares $d(a,b)+1$ with $d'$.

chapters.title: Optimal Matrix-Chain Multiplication
chapters.subtitle: Partition choices with two required subproblems
chapters.summary: Each split requires both child intervals. Black partition nodes represent this joint dependency; increasing interval length gives the bottom-up order.
chapters.state: $(i,j)$, an interval of the matrix chain
chapters.goal: Minimize the scalar multiplications needed to evaluate the chain.
chapters.base: An interval containing one matrix has cost $0$.

blocks.title: Problem overview and examples
blocks.body: {\sffamily\fontsize{7.7}{8.7}\selectfont \textbf{Problem.} Parenthesize a compatible matrix chain so the number of scalar multiplications is minimized; matrix order may not change.\par\vspace{1.5mm}\textbf{Example 1 (used below).} Dimensions $[4,2,3,1,2,5]$ for $ABCDE$ $\rightarrow$ cost $44$, ordering $(A(BC))(DE)$.\par\vspace{1mm}\textbf{Example 2.} Dimensions $[10,30,5,60]$ for $ABC$ $\rightarrow$ cost $4500$, ordering $(AB)C$.\par}

blocks.title: Block 01 -- recursive code
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{7.2}{8.0}\selectfont State $(i,j)$ is the subchain $A_i\cdots A_j$. Repeated states remain separate recursive calls.\par\vspace{1mm}}{\ttfamily\fontsize{6.8}{7.6}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{from\ math\ import\ inf}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{DIMS\ =\ [4,\ 2,\ 3,\ 1,\ 2,\ 5]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ matrix\_chain(i,\ j):}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ case:\ one\ matrix\ needs\ no\ multiplication.}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{if\ i\ ==\ j:}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{return\ 0}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{\#\ Partition\ choices:\ split\ between\ k\ and\ k\ +\ 1.}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{best\ =\ inf}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{for\ k\ in\ range(i,\ j):}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{left\ =\ matrix\_chain(i,\ k)}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{right\ =\ matrix\_chain(k\ +\ 1,\ j)}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{multiply\ =\ DIMS[i\ -\ 1]\ *\ DIMS[k]\ *\ DIMS[j]}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{candidate\ =\ left\ +\ right\ +\ multiply}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{best\ =\ min(best,\ candidate)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{return\ best}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(matrix\_chain(1,\ 5))\ \ \#\ 44}\par
}
blocks.footer: Each candidate adds both subchain costs and the cost of their final multiplication.

blocks.footer: 81 call occurrences and 40 partition nodes. Blue: $k=1$ (66); purple: $k=2$ (109); gold: $k=3$ (44, optimal); teal: $k=4$ (62). Bold gold: $(A(BC))(DE)$. Bold teal: $((A(BC))D)E$. Repeated $(i,j)$ circles are distinct calls; a partition requires both child branches.

blocks.title: DP Block 01 -- bottom-up code
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{7.0}{7.8}\selectfont The table stores cost and ordering. Code indices are zero-based; diagram interval labels are one-based.\par\vspace{1mm}}{\ttfamily\fontsize{6.2}{6.9}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{from\ math\ import\ inf}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{DIMS\ =\ [4,\ 2,\ 3,\ 1,\ 2,\ 5]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{N\ =\ len(DIMS)\ -\ 1}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{NAME\ =\ "ABCDE"}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{cost\ =\ [[inf]\ *\ N\ for\ \_\ in\ range(N)]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{order\ =\ [[""]\ *\ N\ for\ \_\ in\ range(N)]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ cases:\ a\ single\ matrix\ costs\ nothing.}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{for\ i\ in\ range(N):}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{cost[i][i]\ =\ 0}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{order[i][i]\ =\ NAME[i]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ Fill\ successive\ diagonals:\ chain\ lengths\ 2,\ 3,\ ...,\ N.}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{for\ length\ in\ range(2,\ N\ +\ 1):}\par
\hspace*{1.88em}\mbox{for\ i\ in\ range(N\ -\ length\ +\ 1):}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{j\ =\ i\ +\ length\ -\ 1}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{\#\ Choices:\ place\ the\ final\ multiplication\ after\ k.}\par
\hspace*{3.76em}\mbox{for\ k\ in\ range(i,\ j):}\par
\hspace*{5.64em}\mbox{multiply\ =\ DIMS[i]\ *\ DIMS[k\ +\ 1]\ *\ DIMS[j\ +\ 1]}\par
\hspace*{5.64em}\mbox{candidate\ =\ cost[i][k]\ +\ cost[k\ +\ 1][j]\ +\ multiply}\par
\hspace*{5.64em}\mbox{if\ candidate\ <\ cost[i][j]:}\par
\hspace*{7.52em}\mbox{cost[i][j]\ =\ candidate}\par
\hspace*{7.52em}\mbox{left\ =\ order[i][k]\ if\ i\ ==\ k\ else\ f"(\{order[i][k]\})"}\par
\hspace*{7.52em}\mbox{right\ =\ order[k\ +\ 1][j]\ if\ k\ +\ 1\ ==\ j\ else\ f"(\{order[k\ +\ 1][j]\})"}\par
\hspace*{7.52em}\mbox{order[i][j]\ =\ left\ +\ right}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(cost[0][N\ -\ 1],\ order[0][N\ -\ 1])}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ 44\ (A(BC))(DE)}\par
}
blocks.footer: Increasing chain length makes both child intervals available before each update: $O(N^3)$ time, $O(N^2)$ space.

chapters.title: Tower of Hanoi: Arbitrary Legal States
chapters.subtitle: A cyclic state graph and its target-directed optimal DAG
chapters.summary: The start and target may be any legal configurations. The complete graph contains cycles; directing only moves that reduce target distance exposes an optimal DAG.
chapters.goal: Reach an arbitrary fixed target configuration in the minimum moves.
chapters.base: The target returns $0$; a state already on the current path returns $\infty$.

blocks.title: Problem, representation, and examples
Recursive code: six legal actions and path-local cycle rejection
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{6.7}{7.4}\selectfont All six semantic actions appear explicitly. The global set is marked on entry and unmarked on return, so it describes only the current path.}\par\vspace{.8mm}
{\ttfamily\fontsize{6.05}{6.67}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{from\ math\ import\ inf}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ Each\ peg\ is\ stored\ bottom-to-top;\ a\ smaller\ number\ is\ a\ smaller\ disk.}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{START\_LEFT,\ START\_MIDDLE,\ START\_RIGHT\ =\ (2,),\ (3,),\ (1,)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{TARGET\_LEFT,\ TARGET\_MIDDLE,\ TARGET\_RIGHT\ =\ (3,),\ (2,),\ (1,)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\#\ The\ only\ non-constant\ global:\ states\ on\ the\ current\ recursion\ path.}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{VISITED\ =\ set()}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ can\_move(source\_peg,\ destination\_peg):}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{if\ not\ source\_peg:}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{return\ False}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{return\ not\ destination\_peg\ or\ source\_peg[-1]\ <\ destination\_peg[-1]}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ move\_top(source\_peg,\ destination\_peg):}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{disk\ =\ source\_peg[-1]}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{return\ source\_peg[:-1],\ destination\_peg\ +\ (disk,)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ minimum\_moves(left\_peg,\ middle\_peg,\ right\_peg):}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ case:\ the\ arbitrary\ target\ configuration\ has\ been\ reached.}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{if\ (left\_peg\ ==\ TARGET\_LEFT\ and}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{middle\_peg\ ==\ TARGET\_MIDDLE\ and}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{right\_peg\ ==\ TARGET\_RIGHT):}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{return\ 0}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{\#\ Cycle\ base\ case:\ do\ not\ revisit\ a\ state\ on\ this\ branch.}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{state\_key\ =\ (left\_peg,\ middle\_peg,\ right\_peg)}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{if\ state\_key\ in\ VISITED:}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{return\ inf}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{VISITED.add(state\_key)}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{best\ =\ inf}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 1:\ move\ the\ top\ disk\ from\ LEFT\ to\ MIDDLE.}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{if\ can\_move(left\_peg,\ middle\_peg):}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{next\_left,\ next\_middle\ =\ move\_top(left\_peg,\ middle\_peg)}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{best\ =\ min(best,\ 1\ +\ minimum\_moves(}\par
\hspace*{5.04em}\mbox{next\_left,\ next\_middle,\ right\_peg))}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 2:\ move\ the\ top\ disk\ from\ LEFT\ to\ RIGHT.}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{if\ can\_move(left\_peg,\ right\_peg):}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{next\_left,\ next\_right\ =\ move\_top(left\_peg,\ right\_peg)}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{best\ =\ min(best,\ 1\ +\ minimum\_moves(}\par
\hspace*{5.04em}\mbox{next\_left,\ middle\_peg,\ next\_right))}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 3:\ move\ the\ top\ disk\ from\ MIDDLE\ to\ LEFT.}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{if\ can\_move(middle\_peg,\ left\_peg):}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{next\_middle,\ next\_left\ =\ move\_top(middle\_peg,\ left\_peg)}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{best\ =\ min(best,\ 1\ +\ minimum\_moves(}\par
\hspace*{5.04em}\mbox{next\_left,\ next\_middle,\ right\_peg))}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 4:\ move\ the\ top\ disk\ from\ MIDDLE\ to\ RIGHT.}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{if\ can\_move(middle\_peg,\ right\_peg):}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{next\_middle,\ next\_right\ =\ move\_top(middle\_peg,\ right\_peg)}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{best\ =\ min(best,\ 1\ +\ minimum\_moves(}\par
\hspace*{5.04em}\mbox{left\_peg,\ next\_middle,\ next\_right))}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 5:\ move\ the\ top\ disk\ from\ RIGHT\ to\ LEFT.}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{if\ can\_move(right\_peg,\ left\_peg):}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{next\_right,\ next\_left\ =\ move\_top(right\_peg,\ left\_peg)}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{best\ =\ min(best,\ 1\ +\ minimum\_moves(}\par
\hspace*{5.04em}\mbox{next\_left,\ middle\_peg,\ next\_right))}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 6:\ move\ the\ top\ disk\ from\ RIGHT\ to\ MIDDLE.}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{if\ can\_move(right\_peg,\ middle\_peg):}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{next\_right,\ next\_middle\ =\ move\_top(right\_peg,\ middle\_peg)}\par
\hspace*{3.36em}\mbox{best\ =\ min(best,\ 1\ +\ minimum\_moves(}\par
\hspace*{5.04em}\mbox{left\_peg,\ next\_middle,\ next\_right))}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{VISITED.remove(state\_key)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \#\ backtrack\ for\ sibling\ calls}\par
\hspace*{1.68em}\mbox{return\ best}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{print(minimum\_moves(START\_LEFT,\ START\_MIDDLE,\ START\_RIGHT))\ \ \#\ 7}\par
}
blocks.footer: Positive move costs ensure a shortest route is simple. With VISITED initially empty, exhaustive recursion finds its length.

chapters.title: Two Sets II: Three Formulations
chapters.subtitle: The same counting problem represented by three different state semantics
chapters.summary: Fixed identities, sorted sums, and current/other roles give three coordinate systems for the same count. The subtrees compare how choices change those coordinates.
chapters.state: $(i,x,y)$, with formulation-specific meanings for the two sums
chapters.base: Overshooting returns $0$; when $i>n$, return $1$ iff both sums equal the target.

blocks.title: Problem statement, counting convention, and examples
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{7.3}{8.25}\selectfont
\textbf{Problem.} Count the ways to divide the integers $1,2,\ldots,n$ into
two sets having equal sum. The two final sets are unordered.
\par\vspace{1.5mm}
\textbf{Example 1 (used throughout).} $n=7$, total $28$, target per set $14$.
There are $4$ unordered equal-sum partitions, so the displayed recursions return
$8$ labeled assignments before the final division by $2$.
\par\vspace{1mm}
\textbf{Example 2.} $n=4\rightarrow1$, represented by
$\{1,4\}\mid\{2,3\}$.
\par\vspace{1mm}
\textbf{Example 3.} $n=5\rightarrow0$, because the total is odd.
\par\vspace{1.5mm}
Each state records the next integer $i$ and two sums. The code below assumes
even total sum; odd totals have answer $0$. Each unordered partition has two
labeled assignments, hence division by $2$.
The CSES problem uses modulus $10^9+7$; these small examples use exact counts.}

blocks.title: Two concrete histories viewed through three coordinate systems
Why the three recursive programs return the same count
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{6.8}{7.7}\selectfont
\textbf{Fixed-set symmetry.} Exchanging Set 1 and Set 2 leaves the terminal test
and the pair of recursive choices unchanged, so
$F(i,a,b)=F(i,b,a)$.
\par\vspace{2mm}
\textbf{Canonical coordinates.} $G$ evaluates the same two assignments as $F$,
but rewrites each child in larger/smaller order. This changes the state labels
and can make two separate calls have equal arguments; both branch contributions
remain present.
\par\vspace{2mm}
\textbf{Dynamic coordinates.} $H$ keeps the first coordinate attached to the
most recently selected role. Its second branch calls $H(i+1,O+i,C)$; applying
the symmetry of $F$ shows that this reordered call has the same continuation
count as the corresponding fixed-set call.
\par\vspace{2mm}
The counts agree; coordinate normalization does not remove either branch's
contribution.}

blocks.title: Recursive code: fixed Set 1 and Set 2
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{5.7}{6.45}\selectfont The two sum positions have permanent identities. Sending an integer to one set never changes the interpretation of either parameter.}\par\vspace{1.2mm}{\ttfamily\fontsize{4.55}{5.17}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{N\ =\ 7}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{TARGET\ =\ N\ *\ (N\ +\ 1)\ //\ 4}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ count\_fixed(i,\ set1\_sum,\ set2\_sum):}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ cases}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{if\ set1\_sum\ >\ TARGET\ or\ set2\_sum\ >\ TARGET:}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{return\ 0}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{if\ i\ >\ N:}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{return\ int(set1\_sum\ ==\ TARGET\ and}\par
\hspace*{7.60em}\mbox{set2\_sum\ ==\ TARGET)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 1:\ send\ i\ to\ permanently\ named\ Set\ 1.}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{send\_set1\ =\ count\_fixed(}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{i\ +\ 1,\ set1\_sum\ +\ i,\ set2\_sum)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 2:\ send\ i\ to\ permanently\ named\ Set\ 2.}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{send\_set2\ =\ count\_fixed(}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{i\ +\ 1,\ set1\_sum,\ set2\_sum\ +\ i)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{return\ send\_set1\ +\ send\_set2}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{answer\ =\ count\_fixed(1,\ 0,\ 0)\ //\ 2}\par
}\par\vspace{1.3mm}{\sffamily\bfseries\fontsize{6.1}{6.8}\selectfont Invariant: parameter identity is permanent}\par\vspace{.7mm}{\sffamily\fontsize{5.45}{6.15}\selectfont
$a$ is always the sum of Set 1 and $b$ is always the sum of Set 2.
The relation $F(i,a,b)=F(i,b,a)$ is mathematically valid, but this formulation
does not use it to rename or merge calls.
\par\vspace{2mm}
Consequently, $F(3,1,2)$ and $F(3,2,1)$ are symmetric but distinct recursive
calls. The membership labels remain attached to the same named sets.}

blocks.title: Selected subtree: memberships stay attached to A and B
blocks.footer: Gold traces $1\to A$, $2\to B$, $3\to A$. Set membership and parameter identity agree throughout.

blocks.title: Recursive code: normalize both children
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{5.7}{6.45}\selectfont Each choice adds to a role, then sorts the two resulting sums. The actual sets keep their elements while their L/S names may change.}\par\vspace{1.2mm}{\ttfamily\fontsize{4.55}{5.17}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{N\ =\ 7}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{TARGET\ =\ N\ *\ (N\ +\ 1)\ //\ 4}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ normalize(x,\ y):}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{return\ max(x,\ y),\ min(x,\ y)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ count\_large\_small(i,\ large,\ small):}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ cases}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{if\ large\ >\ TARGET:}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{return\ 0}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{if\ i\ >\ N:}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{return\ int(large\ ==\ TARGET\ and}\par
\hspace*{7.60em}\mbox{small\ ==\ TARGET)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 1:\ add\ i\ to\ the\ set\ currently\ called\ L.}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{next\_large,\ next\_small\ =\ normalize(large\ +\ i,\ small)}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{send\_large\ =\ count\_large\_small(}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{i\ +\ 1,\ next\_large,\ next\_small)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 2:\ add\ i\ to\ the\ set\ currently\ called\ S.}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{next\_large,\ next\_small\ =\ normalize(large,\ small\ +\ i)}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{send\_small\ =\ count\_large\_small(}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{i\ +\ 1,\ next\_large,\ next\_small)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{return\ send\_large\ +\ send\_small}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{answer\ =\ count\_large\_small(1,\ 0,\ 0)\ //\ 2}\par
}\par\vspace{1.3mm}{\sffamily\bfseries\fontsize{6.1}{6.8}\selectfont Invariant: numerical order, not set identity}\par\vspace{.7mm}{\sffamily\fontsize{5.45}{6.15}\selectfont
$L\ge S$ at every call. If adding $i$ to the smaller sum makes it larger, the
next call interchanges the two coordinate roles.
\par\vspace{2mm}
At the root, ``put 1 in L'' and ``put 1 in S, then normalize'' both call
$G(2,1,0)$. The plain recursion evaluates both calls; their two contributions
must still be added.}

blocks.title: Selected subtree: normalization can interchange L and S
blocks.footer: The two root children are drawn separately because there is no memoization; the equality annotation records multiplicity, not merging.

blocks.title: Recursive code: the recipient becomes current
blocks.body:
{\sffamily\fontsize{5.7}{6.45}\selectfont Choosing current preserves the roles. Choosing other adds i to O and passes that recipient first in the next recursive call.}\par\vspace{1.2mm}{\ttfamily\fontsize{4.55}{5.17}\selectfont\raggedright
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{N\ =\ 7}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{TARGET\ =\ N\ *\ (N\ +\ 1)\ //\ 4}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{def\ count\_current\_other(i,\ current,\ other):}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{\#\ Base\ cases}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{if\ current\ >\ TARGET\ or\ other\ >\ TARGET:}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{return\ 0}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{if\ i\ >\ N:}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{return\ int(current\ ==\ TARGET\ and}\par
\hspace*{7.60em}\mbox{other\ ==\ TARGET)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 1:\ current\ receives\ i\ and\ keeps\ its\ role.}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{send\_current\ =\ count\_current\_other(}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{i\ +\ 1,\ current\ +\ i,\ other)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{\#\ Choice\ 2:\ other\ receives\ i\ and\ becomes\ current.}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{send\_other\ =\ count\_current\_other(}\par
\hspace*{3.20em}\mbox{i\ +\ 1,\ other\ +\ i,\ current)}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{1.60em}\mbox{return\ send\_current\ +\ send\_other}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{\strut}\par
\hspace*{0.00em}\mbox{answer\ =\ count\_current\_other(1,\ 0,\ 0)\ //\ 2}\par
}\par\vspace{1.3mm}{\sffamily\bfseries\fontsize{6.1}{6.8}\selectfont Invariant: role follows the action, not magnitude}\par\vspace{.7mm}{\sffamily\fontsize{5.45}{6.15}\selectfont
The second branch is $H(i+1,O+i,C)$: the recipient becomes current and the old
current becomes other. No sorting occurs.
\par\vspace{2mm}
Therefore $C$ may be less than $O$. This distinguishes $H$ from $G$ even when a
short history happens to produce the same numeric tuple. Equal root arguments
again remain two recursive calls.}

blocks.title: Selected subtree: choosing other explicitly rotates the roles
blocks.footer: The lower contrast branch shows H(5,4,6): current is smaller, which cannot occur in the canonical large/small formulation.

blocks.title: Reading the same choices across F, G, and H
